Lungs In 50% of rats immunized with S protein alveolar epithelial hyperplasia was identified (Table , Fig. a,c, Fig. a–c). Mitotic figures (Fig. c) and binucleated cells (Fig. c) can occasionally be found in foci of alveolar epithelial hyperplasia. As it is known, alveolar epithelial hyperplasia is a proliferation of cuboidal type II pneumocytes , . Since type II pneumocytes express ACE2, we expected an increase in the number of ACE2 positive cells in hyperplastic foci. However, only a few cuboidal type II pneumocytes in the focus of hyperplasia were stained with antibodies against ACE2 (Fig. a). The type II pneumocytes have the capacity to transdifferentiate into type I pneumocytes. Within the process of transdifferentiation, type II cells dedifferentiate, proliferate and some of the daughter cells differentiate into type I cells . Jia et al. have shown that the expression of ACE2 in type II pneumocytes positively correlates with the state of cell differentiation. Undifferentiated cells express little ACE2 . We assumed that the unstained cells in hyperplastic foci are type II pneumocytes, undergoing dedifferentiation and proliferation. Staining for surfactant-associated protein C (SP-C), which is known to be type II pneumocyte-specific marker, showed single type II pneumocytes in hyperplastic foci (Fig. a,b). Hyperplastic foci were clearly negative for aquaporin AQP5, which is type I pneumocytes marker (Fig. c), whereas non-hyperplastic areas of the lung in the same section showed strong staining for anti-AQP5 (Fig. d). Thus, hyperplastic foci mainly contain cells, which bear neither type II pneumocytes markers (ACE-2 and SP-C) nor type I pneumocytes marker (AQP5). The morphological analysis of hyperplastic cells showed that they combine features of both type I and type II pneumocytes. These cells exhibited round nuclei and residual lamellar bodies with positive staining for SP-C, features consistent with type II pneumocytes (Fig. b). Unlike type II pneumocytes, the cells exhibited asymmetrically located nuclei and were larger in diameter (12–17 µm) (Fig. b). Moreover, hyperplastic cells had pure cytoplasm similar to type I pneumocytes (Fig. b). Hyperplastic cells in lungs of rats immunized with S protein are likely to be transitional cells, which were described in diverse mouse models of lung injury and in postmortem lung tissue of patients with COVID-19 acute respiratory distress syndrome . Transitional cells refer to type II pneumocytes that have proliferated in an attempt to replace damaged alveolar epithelial cells, but failed to complete trans-differentiation into type I pneumocytes . The transitional state is characterized by markers of cell cycle exit, down-regulation of type 2 pneumocyte markers (ACE-2 and SP-C), absence of type 1 pneumocyte markers, a cuboidal or partially spread morphology, and expression of unique signature genes, including KRT8 . Immunostaining of rat lung sections for CD3, CD4, CD8 and CD45RA revealed the infiltration of CD4 + T lymphocytes and CD45RA + B lymphocytes (Fig. ). Therefore, we cannot rule out that alveolar type II pneumocyte hyperplasia is caused not only by serum autoantibodies to ACE2, but also by antibodies locally produced by infiltrating B cells. In addition to lymphocytic infiltration in lung parenchyma, 2 out of 10 rats immunized with S protein revealed perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and lymphocytic infiltration in the walls of lung vessels (Fig. ). Thus, immunization with SARS-CoV-2 S protein caused alveolar hyperplasia in rats. The foci of hyperplastic alveolar epithelium consist of dedifferentiated type II pneumocyte, contain atypical cells, T and B lymphocytic infiltrates. Discussion Histological analysis of the lungs and kidneys of rats immunized with SARS-CoV-2 S protein revealed hyperplasia and dedifferentiation of type II pneumocytes in the lungs, CD4 + T, CD45RA + lymphocytic infiltration and perivascular lymphocytic infiltration in the lungs, thinning or loss of brush border and destruction of epithelial cells of the proximal renal tubules, CD4 + T and CD8 + T lymphocytic infiltration in areas of proximal tubule damage. We compared the lesions detected in rats with the histopathology detected in COVID-19 patients. Hammoud et al. summarizing 50 articles reporting organ pathology in COVID-19 patients showed that pneumocyte hyperplasia and lymphocyte and/or monocyte infiltrates were found in 60% of cases . The review of articles made by Malik et al. proves that type II pneumocyte hyperplasia is one of the most common shared findings among lung-histological sections of COVID-19 patients . Hammoud et al. summarizing 50 articles reporting organ pathology in COVID-19 patients showed that pneumocyte hyperplasia and lymphocyte and/or monocyte infiltrates were found in 60% of cases . The review of articles made by Malik et al. proves that type II pneumocyte hyperplasia is one of the most common shared findings among lung-histological sections of COVID-19 patients . Zeng et al. found perivascular inflammatory infiltration in the lungs of COVID-19 patient . Patients who died of COVID-19 showed clinical signs of kidney injury that included increased serum creatinine and/or new-onset proteinuria. By light microscopy, proximal acute tubule injury manifested as the loss of brush border, vacuolar degeneration, dilatation of the tubular lumen with cellular debris, and occasionally even frank necrosis and detachment of epithelium with bare tubular basement membrane were noted , . Larsen et al. found damage to the epithelium of the proximal tubules, which included reactive nuclei with mitotic figures and diffuse simplification with the exposure of brush edges in the deceased patient . Consequently, the lesions found in the lungs and kidneys of S protein immunized rats are similar to those found in COVID-19 patients. The mechanism of kidney and lung damage during SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans remains unclear. Viral particles in kidneys were not identified and prominent interstitial inflammation characteristic of many viral nephropathies was not seen in people died from COVID-19 . The RNA of the virus in the kidneys of dead people was also not detected. These facts raise doubts that the cause of tissue damage in SARS-CoV-2 infection is the direct effect of the virus on cells. Induction of SARS-CoV-2 infection-specific damage in rats by S protein immunization without SARS-CoV-2 infection indicates that organ damage is caused by autoimmune reaction induced by viral S protein. Both type II pneumocytes and epithelial cells of the proximal tubules of the kidneys express ACE2. Damage to ACE2 expressing cells in the absence of other obvious damage of the studied organs in rats immunized with S protein indicates that the target of an autoimmune attack induced by S protein immunization is ACE2. Geanes et al. demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 infection can increase autoantibody levels to ACE2 . The levels of these autoantibodies were associated with COVID-19 disease severity , . At the same time, no deposits of immunoglobulins were found in the kidneys . We also found the production of autoantibodies to ACE2 in rats immunized with S protein. Induction of autoreactive lymphocytes to ACE2 may occur via their idiotype–anti-idiotypic interactions with lymphocytes specific to SARS-CoV-2 S protein. Existence of idiotype–anti-idiotypic interactions between autoreactive lymphocytes to ACE2 and lymphocytes to SARS-CoV-2 S protein is likely to take place, as SARS-CoV-2 S protein and ACE2 are complementary . However, no relationship was found between production of autoantibodies to ACE2 and the degree of damage to ACE2 expressing cells. Moreover, in a few rats immunized with S protein, lung and kidney damage occurred in the absence of production of autoantibodies to ACE2. At the same time, infiltration of CD4 + T lymphocytes and CD45RA + B lymphocytes was observed in damaged rat lungs. As is well known, B lymphocytes infiltrating lesion sites may produce disease-specific autoantibodies in some autoimmune diseases . Based on these facts, we assume that the damage of ACE2-expressing cells in the lungs may be caused not only by serum autoantibodies to ACE2 but also by autoantibodies locally produced by infiltrating B cells. The CD4 + T and CD8 + T lymphocyte infiltration observed in the kidneys suggests the key role of anti-idiotypic T cell-mediated autoimmune response against ACE2 in the damage of ACE2-expressing epithelial cells in the kidneys. In human an inflammatory infiltrate was also detected in the interstitial cortex of the kidneys, which consisted of lymphocytes and plasma cells with scattered eosinophils . Not only infection, but also mRNA vaccination with the COVID-19 vaccine can lead to T lymphocytic and macrophage infiltration in the lungs, kidneys, pericardium and myocardium, gastrointestinal tract, bladder and diaphragm, including fatal – . The chronic exposure of a target organ to a complex cytokine mixture, produced by T lymphocytes, could have varying consequences depending on the organ. Target cells could be killed by T lymphocytes. Alternatively, cytokines may alter the normal growth and differentiation of target cells leading to abnormal growth or deficits in cell populations . Conclusion SARS-CoV-2 S protein immunization induces autoimmune reaction attacking ACE2- expressing cells, as a result of which type II pneumocytes undergo hyperplasia and dedifferentiation, epithelial cells of the proximal tubules of the kidneys are destroyed.

Introduction Generic drugs are made to be chemically and therapeutically equivalent to the brand name ones. These equivalencies are obtained at lower costs making generic drugs use certainly appealing. Therefore, many payers/providers have encouraged substitution of brand name drugs with inexpensive bioequivalent generic versions [ ]. In the last 30 years, several controversies concerning generic drugs legislation have arisen. Recent literature reviews demonstrated that physicians, pharmacists and general population hold negative perceptions and knowledge of generic medicines [ - ]. Neuromuscular Blocking Agents (NMBAs) are usually used in patients with altered respiratory mechanics properties such as Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), status asthmaticus or severe acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) [ , ]. Only few products exhibit the so called ideal Neuromuscular Blockade (NMB) effect which is influenced by several factors namely, required speed of onset and offset, cardiovascular stability, possible accumulation of the NMBA metabolites, elimination routes, and costs [ , ]. One of these products is cisatracurium which is a non-depolarizing NMBA, a benzylisoquinolinium like atracurium, doxacurium, and mivacurium [ ]. Since its introduction in the early 2000, cisatracurium was widely used in Intensive Care Units (ICUs) in developed countries. However, it generated relatively high costs [ ]. Here and there several cisatracurium generics have been developed to respond to the need of lowering expenses. Cisatracurium became of relatively frequent use in critical care, taking advantage of its higher potency and limited side effects [ ]. Payen et al . [ ], reported that NMBAs were used in 9% of patients on day two, 7% on day four and 5% on day six. Cisatracurium accounted for 70% of NMBA use. In developing as in developed countries, cisatracurium use remained rather sporadic [ ]. Recently the introduction of Cisatrex®, the generic of the brand name Nimbex®, provided an opportunity to substitute commonly used NMBAs for cisatracurium. Because of the physicians´ reluctance to prescribe generics due to different controversies, authors hypothesized that a proof of safety and efficacy of Cisatrex® compared to its brand-name could reassure intensivists. The aim of the present study was to compare efficacy and tolerance of two marketed forms, brand-name (Nimbex®) and generic name (Cisatrex®) of cisatracurium-induced paralysis in hypoxemic ventilated patients. Methods Study design and setting: this was a crossover randomized double-blind physiological study conducted in an 8-bed Medical ICU from February 2015 to March 2016, which compared neuromuscular blockade efficacy and tolerance induced respectively by continuous perfusion of brand-name (Nimbex®) and generic name (Cisatrex®) of cisatracurium during two successive time periods. Inclusion criteria: patients admitted to the ICU for severe acute respiratory failure with severe hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 < 200mmHg), presenting important patient-ventilator asynchrony under invasive mechanical ventilation, despite deep analgo-sedation as assessed by Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) [ ], were enrolled when drug induced paralysis was required. Patients with history of allergy to cisatracurium, malignant hyperthermia, pregnancy, neuromuscular disorders or hemodynamic instability, were not included in the present study. Discussion The present randomized double-blind crossover study which investigated the efficacy and the tolerance of two forms of cisatracurium (brand name Nimbex® and generic Cisatrex®) demonstrated no significant differences in the paralysis, the recovery times or in tolerance in hypoxemic mechanically ventilated critically ill patients. To the best of the authors´ knowledge (relying on recent PubMed searches accessed on March 2019, between 1966 and March 2019, using the following MeSH words: cisatracurium, generic, brand, bioequivalence), the present study would be the first to address the issue related to the comparison between the bioequivalence and the pharmacodynamics properties regarding the brand-name and the generic of cisatracurium. This was a randomized double-blind crossover study. This design is highly adapted to this kind of physiological studies aimed at demonstrating differences in paralysis and recovery delays between the two studied forms of cisatracurium [ , ]. In the present study, the calculated sample size estimated at 22 is satisfactory compared to several studies including samples ranging from 6 to 37 patients [ , , , - ] ( ). All patients presenting an indication for paralysis within the study period were included. Indeed, the sample was featured by a large proportion of COPD patients compared to the more classical indication mainly ARDS patients [ ]. The relatively high proportion of COPD patients is explained by the particular recruitment of this spectrum of severe AE/COPD patients presenting at ICU admission with a clinical picture characterized by a severe obstructive disorder generating major patient ventilator asynchrony. The relatively low median PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) may be explained by the important proportion of COPD patients in whom PEEP was set at zero. Indeed, this could be revealed by the elevated median autoPEEP. The TOF, used in the present study to monitor the paralysis in response to both studied drugs, is one among the most commonly used methods [ ]. Indeed, the TOF proved to be one of the most balanced tools between the monitoring of the paralysis delay and the recovery time [ ]. Typical fade of the TOF response defines competitive NMB by nondepolarizing NMBAs. The cutoff of TOF below 2/4 used to define the paralysis delay was chosen according to the study by Lagneau et al . [ ], which demonstrated the clinical relevance and safety of this cutoff when compared to a TOF at 0/4. These data were thereafter confirmed by the 2002 “Clinical Practice Guidelines for Sustained Neuromuscular Blockade in the Adult Critically Ill Patient” updated in 2016 [ , ]. This study presents three limitations. The first limitation concerns the difficulty to assess sharply the TOF recovery time, in a narrow spectrum of patients presenting rather decreasing in the amplitude of contractions. The co-investigator (NF) was well trained to this task especially via the pre-protocol patient. Otherwise, the crossover design was sufficient to offset this limitation. The second limitation is, when introducing cisatracurium, a bolus is usually administered before the continuous infusion [ , , ]. This bolus has not been used in the protocol to allow a progressive decrease of the TOF and thus the comparison of the decline of the TOF and the paralysis time delays to reach a TOF of 2/4. One could rather consider the design Bolus 1- Monitoring of Recovery - Washout period - Bolus 2 - Monitoring of Recovery to be interesting at least in regard of the aim of the study. Two arguments could be developed for this. First, as clinical considerations, patients with oxygenation deficit (severe ARDS) as well as decarboxylation deficit (AECOPD, Asthma) and need of relaxation to improve ventilation will definitely gain profit from an immediate relaxation, rather than a progressive one displayed over two hours

Second, as pharmacological considerations, the wash out of middle-long NDMR (non-depolarizing MR) like cisatracurium are more Dose-Dependent and less Time-of-Application-Dependent (when given continuously). That means by the time of stopping the IV-application, starts the wash out period, which is about (45-50 min) [ , - ]. The problem is, a clinical TOF-recovery is not linear to the pharmacological recovery. Most current NDMR from Benzylisochinolin family or from Steroidal family have, a) a dose-effect-ratio around 70-75%, which means that 70-75% of the Acetylcholine receptors (ACh-receptors) have to be engaged/bound to have a clinically apparent muscle relaxation. b) an autonomic-safety-reserve (= the ratio of neuromuscular blocking-dose needed to expect the muscarinic effect = dose needed to effect observed) set up high (Example 20: 1 for vecuronium) in comparison to depolarizing MR or old MR. Meaning that 20 time the MR dose needed for the effect is given IV. This is to have a reserve in deploying the MR effect [ ]. Both effect 1 and 2 means in reverse conclusion, that an observed clinical recovery in muscle relaxation (TOF-based) after one hour can just mean that 30% of the receptors are free, but maybe most of them are still bound by the MR. This has normally no clinical relevance in intensive care (compare to anesthesiology or emergency care), but applying a new drug after this one hour, based on the sole clinical recovery can lead to interaction between the rest-MR of the first arm of the study, and the second one. The blood levels of the first medication has not been sampled prior to the application of the second MR in this study, so that it remains unclear at what pharmacological levels of the first the second one has been applied, and interact with the first one. Actually, in clinical routine, this must NOT be done, but in respect to the kinetic of MR-binding biology, a greater wash-out period would have reduced the risk of drug interactions, which can bias the results in a cross-over design. The random order could, although, have lessened the difference. Another possibility could have been to start with a bolus followed by a predefined low continuous infusion regimen (i.e. 0.06mg.kg -1 .h -1 ) for the two studied drugs, then monitor the TOF increase. But we have to define the dosing regimen, and the effect of the bolus could largely delay the procedure and thus alter the benefit of the cross-over design. The third limitation regarding the monitoring of the paralysis, is that clinical parameters, ventilatory parameters and patient-ventilator asynchronies have been just studied to ascertain that patients presented no significant asynchronies and were clinically well paralyzed. Conclusion The present study demonstrated the equipotent effect of two marketed forms of cisatracurium (brand name Nimbex® and generic Cisatrex®) in hypoxemic mechanically ventilated critically ill patients. Indeed, both forms displayed equivalent paralysis delays and recovery kinetics. Tolerance was also equivalent as demonstrated by the absence of significant variations of cardio-circulatory parameters. What is known about this topic In developing countries as in many others, cisatracurium-use remained rather modest because of economic considerations; Recently the introduction of Cisatrex®, the generic of the brand name Nimbex®, provided an opportunity to substitute cisatracurium to other neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs); Physicians’ reluctance to prescribe generics may impede their use, because of all the surrounding controversies, involving generic drugs legislation especially the approval process, issues of bioequivalence and corruption that have arisen. What this study adds Authors hypothesized that a proof of safety and efficacy of Cisatrex® compared to its original brand-name could be of an invaluable support to reassure the intensivist while using Cisatrex® This is a crossover double-blind randomized study to compare efficacy and tolerance of two marketed forms, brand-name (Nimbex®) and generic (Cisatrex®) of continuous cisatracurium-induced paralysis in hypoxemic ventilated patients in a medical intensive care unit; The present study revealed no significant differences in efficacy as in tolerance between brand-name Nimbex® and generic Cisatrex® of cisatracurium continuous infusion in hypoxemic ventilated patients.

The quality of survival for patients after intensive care unit (ICU) admission is a major health challenge that has been described as the defining challenge for critical care in the 21st century. ICU survivors may have delayed and compromised functional recovery, which can persist for months or years. , Preliminary evidence suggests that critically ill patients admitted to an ICU who are expected to require prolonged mechanical ventilation may benefit from early activity and mobilisation. , , The Treatment of Invasively Ventilated Adults with Early Activity and Mobilisation (TEAM III) trial ( ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT03133377 ) is a phase 3 randomised controlled trial of patients who are expected to receive mechanical ventilation for more than 48 hours. In these patients, we will evaluate whether, compared with standard care, early mobilisation and rehabilitation commenced in the ICU increases the number of days alive and out of hospital at 180 days (DAOH 180 ) after randomisation. In this article, we describe the protocol and statistical analysis plan, which was finalised before completion of trial patient recruitment. Methods Study design and setting TEAM III is an international, multicentre, prospective, parallel-group, randomised controlled phase 3 superiority trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of an early activity and mobilisation protocol compared with standard care. The first patient was randomly assigned in February 2018 and patient recruitment is estimated to be completed by October 2021. Final collection of all 180-day outcome data is anticipated by May 2022. The total recruitment target of 750 patients will be enrolled from sites in Australia, New Zealand, Germany, Ireland, the United Kingdom and Brazil. Study population The inclusion and exclusion criteria are shown in . Eligible patients will be randomly assigned to early activity and mobilisation, to the highest suitable level as assessed daily by a physiotherapist face to face during the ICU admission up to 28 days, or physiotherapy care that is standard for that hospital. Randomisation A web-based interface ( https://www.teamtrial.org.au ) will be used to confirm that patients fulfil all the inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria. Randomisation between trial mobilisation and control interventions will be performed on this website using a computer-generated randomised treatment allocation schedule stratified by participating hospital site with a permuted scheme with blocks of varying sizes. Treatment masking (blinding) Patient mobility while receiving mechanical ventilation is obvious, so it is not possible to blind patients or clinical staff to treatment allocation. Bias will be minimised by concealed treatment allocation before randomisation, protocolised treatment of the intervention group, and assessment of the primary outcome by centralised, blinded and trained research staff in each region. In the United Kingdom, minimisation of bias will be augmented by data linkage. The primary outcome measure — number of DAOH 180 after randomisation, with any days spent in a rehabilitation facility or nursing home counted as days in hospital — is subject to minimal ascertainment bias. Intervention We followed the UK’s Medical Research Council guidelines for developing and evaluating a complex intervention and the template for intervention description and replication (TIDieR) checklist and guide ( ). , Each patient allocated to the intervention group will receive physiotherapist-directed, functional rehabilitation comprising active exercises and mobilisation conducted as early as possible and at the highest level of ICU mobility scale activity possible for them ( ; ). , The first full day will be considered Day 1 and the intervention will occur daily for the duration of the ICU stay up to Day 28. Each patient allocated to the control group will receive standard care from physiotherapy staff not involved in delivering the intervention, which in most cases will involve no active exercise out of bed. For both groups, concomitant care will be guided by the treating clinician and all post-ICU patient management will be at the discretion of the patient’s ward-based treating physicians. The intervention and study tools were designed to facilitate updates to clinical practice if the TEAM III trial results support such implementation. Primary outcome The trial primary outcome variable will be DAOH 180 . , , For each patient, days during the index hospitalisation, hospital readmission, inpatient rehabilitation or in a nursing home between randomisation and Day 180 will be subtracted from 180 to calculate their DAOH 180 result ( ). Patients who die before Day 180 will be defined as having the worst possible outcome of zero DAOH 180 . Secondary outcomes Secondary outcome measures will be evaluated at 28 days and 180 days after randomisation ( ). Outcomes at Day 28 include: all-cause mortality; ICU-free days; ventilator-free days; and delirium-free days measured using the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) and Richmond Agitation–Sedation Scale (RASS). Patients who die before Day 28 will be assigned zero ICU-free, ventilator-free and delirium-free days. Outcomes at Day 180 include: all-cause mortality; time to death; DAOH

Outcomes at Day 180 include: all-cause mortality; time to death; DAOH in patients who die before Day 180; DAOH in patients alive at Day 180; days in hospital, a rehabilitation facility or a nursing home to Day 180 according to 180-day survival status; quality of life and health status measured using the five-level EuroQol five dimensions questionnaire (EQ-5D-5L); independent activities of daily living scores measured using the Barthel activities of daily living (ADL) index and the Lawton instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) scale; generic function and disability measured using the 12-level World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0 12L); cognitive function measured using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MOCA)–Blind; and psychological function measured using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) and Impact of Event Scale – Revised (IES-R). Statistical analyses Effect estimates for all outcomes will be accompanied by a 95% confidence interval (CI), consistent with a two-sided type 1 error of 5%. There will be no adjustment for multiplicity of testing among effect estimates and corresponding 95% CIs for non-primary outcomes, which therefore should be interpreted cautiously as hypothesis-generating results. Descriptive and summary statistics will be calculated by treatment group and overall. Continuous data will be summarised as means (standard deviations [SDs]) if about normally distributed, and otherwise as medians (interquartile ranges). Categorical data will be summarised as counts and proportions. Unadjusted differences between groups will be assessed initially using two-sample t tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, or Fisher exact tests for proportions, as appropriate. The number of screened patients who fulfil the inclusion criteria, the numbers included in the primary and secondary analyses and all reasons for exclusion from the primary and secondary analyses will be reported according to CONSORT guidelines ( ). The full analysis set for the main primary and secondary analyses will retain participants in their original randomly assigned groups, and include all randomly assigned patients except those who withdraw consent for use of trial data. , Wherever possible and appropriate, statistical inference will account for potential dependency in patient clusters formed by each participating ICU or hospital site. Linear and generalised linear model diagnostics, outlier assessment and remedial measures will follow standard approaches. , Proportional hazards assumptions across treatment arms in time-to-event analyses will be evaluated using scaled Schoenfeld residuals and visual assessment of log–log plots. Whenever needed, the proportional odds assumption for cumulative logistic models will be assessed by visual assessment of relevant plots for clinically important departures from proportionality. Primary outcome The primary outcome, DAOH 180 , is expected to have a bimodal and asymmetric frequency distribution. A linear quantile regression analysis will be used because this approach models selected conditional quantiles of a continuous response. Also, this is potentially more robust to outliers and misspecification of an error distribution compared with traditional least squares linear (mean) regression. DAOH 180 will be modelled as a continuous random variable, with a null hypothesis of equality in the median (quantile = 0.5) DAOH 180 between the full analysis set of patients according to randomised treatment group. The magnitude of the differential primary outcome according to randomised treatment group will be derived from the treatment group effect estimate returned by a simple linear median quantile model with a term for binary treatment group. The number needed to treat for benefit or harm will also be reported if strong evidence of a difference between treatment groups is found. Model fitting will use published software for linear quantile models. At the time of writing, within the R statistical environment, the quantile regression package quantreg offers a bootstrapped procedure for construction of cluster-robust standard errors with associated 95% CIs to support cluster-robust inference ( ). , , Specification of either simplex (exterior point) or interior point median regression methods showed satisfactory relative power compared with several alternative analysis methods in simulated data scenarios ( ). Ordinal categorical analysis The differential effect of treatment will be estimated within a proportional odds cumulative logistic model treating DAOH 180 as an ordinal categorical random variable. The wide range of DAOH 180 categories may be collapsed to a convenient and clinically meaningful smaller number of ordered categories without important loss of statistical information. , , Secondary outcomes Because no adjustment for multiple comparisons will be performed in the analyses of trial secondary outcomes, these outcomes and their reported unadjusted 95% CIs will be considered hypothesis-generating. Time-to-event analyses The time to events of interest, including mortality to 180 days, will be assessed using Kaplan–Meier plots and log-rank tests. These will be supplemented by Cox proportional hazard regression models including variables as for the primary outcome model, with the proportional hazards assumption assessed using Schoenfeld residuals, as described above. The time to discharge according to treatment group will be assessed using a competing risks model with death before discharge treated as a competing risk. Other binary outcomes Other binary variables, including adverse events, will be analysed with logistic regression models to estimate odds ratios with 95% CIs. Pre-specified subgroup analyses of the primary outcome Possible heterogeneity of treatment effect in the following pre-specified subgroups will be evaluated by tests of interaction between each subgroup and the study treatment in the models described above: • baseline WHODAS 2.0 category (no and mild disability versus moderate, severe and complete disability); • age (dichotomised at the full analysis set median age); • diagnosis (sepsis versus trauma versus other); • severity of illness (dichotomised at the full analysis set median APACHE [Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation] III score); and • frailty (a binary reduction of the seven-point Clinical Frailty Scale at 1–4 [well and vulnerable] versus 5–7 [frail]). The new appearance of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection across the world during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic introduces the possibility that these patients may be enrolled in TEAM III in substantial numbers. These patients may have experienced a different clinical trajectory from other ICU patients recruited so far, including prolonged durations of mechanical ventilation accompanied by days of pharmacological paralysis and treatment with glucocorticoid medication. , Using the full analysis set, the primary outcome will also be evaluated according to SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 status subgroup (known positive versus negative or unknown). The WHODAS 2.0 12L percentage scores will be used to categorise patients into five mutually exclusive disability categories at 180 days: no disability (0–4%); mild disability (5–24%); moderate disability (25–49%); severe disability (50–95%); and complete disability (96–100%). In addition, patients will be classified as having no or mild disability if their WHODAS score was < 25%, and classified as moderate, severe or complete disability if their WHODAS score was ≥ 25%. Cost-effectiveness analyses Cost-effectiveness analyses will be conducted from a health care payer perspective using a within-trial time horizon. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios will be calculated as a cost per additional quality-adjusted life-year and cost per additional day alive and out of hospital gained at Day 180 for early activity and mobilisation compared with standard care. The EQ-5D-5L, administered 6 months after randomisation, will enable utilities to be determined and subsequent calculation of quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs). Costs will be determined based on resource use during the intensive care, acute care and post-acute care periods up to Day 180 and will include costs of the intervention where appropriate. To address the issue of transferability in multinational trials, we will adjust for heterogeneity across geographic regions (which may arise, for example, owing to differences in treatment patterns) and obtain estimates for costs and effects in specific regions of the study. All costs will be converted to a common currency using purchasing power parity statistics from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Health care costs will be compared between regions using the same methods as used in previous economic evaluations of multinational clinical trials by our group. Per-protocol analyses It is well understood that trial protocols may not be followed fully for some trial participants. Following completion of the main primary and secondary outcome analyses, there will be an option to repeat a selection of those analyses using a per-protocol analysis set, whereby the subset of protocol-compliant patients assigned to early activity and mobilisation is compared with all patients assigned to the control group. , , Protocol-compliant patients will be determined retrospectively; this will exclude patients for whom there were major protocol violations (eg, violation of entry criteria leading to random assignment of ineligible patients), patients who were not assessed by a physiotherapist for possible early activity and mobilisation on every day from randomisation to ICU discharge (to a maximum of 28 days), and patients for whom the primary outcome variable is not available. Sample size, power and interim analysis schedule Conservative inflation factors were applied to a standard parametric calculation for sample size in this quantile regression. Estimated mean and SD DAOH 180 were derived from a published pilot TEAM randomised controlled trial and systematic review, assuming overall mean ± SD days alive and out of hospital of 143 ± 21 (control group) versus 156 ± 27 (intervention group). , Using a type I error proportion of 0.05 and a 7-day difference between the groups in DAOH 180 (being about half the point estimate found in the pilot randomised controlled trial), recruiting 313 patients in each group would achieve 90% power to detect a difference. The recruitment goal was set at 750 patients. This final trial size incorporated an inflation of 15% to account for a non-parametric distribution of the primary end point and up to a 5% loss to follow-up; in comparison, previous studies by the ANZICS Clinical Trials Group have yielded losses to follow-up of ≤ 2%. , Interim analysis There has been one interim analysis assessing efficacy and safety by the DSMC located in Ireland, the UK and the US, with no early stopping option planned for futility. A time point of 1 month after the first 400 patients reached their 28-day follow-up (3 June 2020) was set so that the interim analysis was conducted in a timely manner. At that point, the DSMC had access to: • differential all-cause mortality at hospital discharge, censored at Day 28; • the differential number of days alive and not in hospital to Day 28, with a score of zero allocated to any survivors who remained in hospital at Day 28; and • the differential number of days alive and not in hospital to Day 180 for those with available data. The DSMC’s interim evaluation of Day 28 censored accumulated differential all-cause mortality at hospital discharge was supported by symmetrical ± 3 SD Haybittle–Peto boundaries, with this interim analysis “spending” a total of 0.0031 of the available type 1 error at that point. To preserve an overall type 1 error no greater than 0.05, the final analysis of the primary trial outcome at full recruitment should be conducted at a two-sided P value of 0.0491 (Z = ± 1.967), which in practice will be assumed unchanged from 0.05. On 2 September 2020, the DSMC confirmed that the TEAM III trial was approved to continue recruitment to the final target sample size. Discussion Invasive mechanical ventilation is a life-saving intervention, but patients receiving this intervention are typically confined to bed with no active exercise. This immobilisation may contribute substantially to the development of muscle weakness and wasting in many such patients, with these undesirable events associated with increased hospital length of stay, increased mortality after hospital discharge, and poor long-term functional recovery. At present, there are no specific proven therapies available for this common clinical scenario. The potential benefits of a bundle of activities comprising early activity and mobilisation during prolonged invasive mechanical ventilation are supported by scientific rationale. This intervention has the potential to shorten ventilator dependence, decrease mortality, and reduce physical and cognitive functional decline associated with illnesses needing prolonged mechanical ventilation in an ICU. The TEAM III trial is designed to detect an important beneficial effect of early activity and mobilisation, if one exists, while minimising potential risks. Application of the statistical analysis plan within this TEAM III trial protocol will facilitate evaluation of these important clinical data and support confidence in the subsequent generalisation of its findings. The aim of the TEAM III trial is to provide definitive guidance for clinicians regarding the true efficacy and safety of a bundle of activities comprising early activity and mobilisation in the management of critical illness in adults. Introduction The growing complexity of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) procedures and the rising evidence of temperature-related endothelial dysfunction underscore a pressing need to reassess standard protocols. This article is motivated by increasing concern about how poorly managed temperature transitions can adversely impact vascular health and patient outcomes. CPB is an indispensable procedure in cardiac surgery that involves extensive manipulation of the patient’s physiological state to facilitate complex surgical interventions while the heart is temporarily stopped. Central to the CPB process is the induction of therapeutic hypothermia, where the patient’s body temperature is deliberately lowered to a range typically between 28°C and 32°C [ , ] . This critical step is not merely about reducing the body’s metabolic rate – it is a protective strategy aimed at safeguarding neurological functions and minimizing the risk of ischemic tissue damage during the period when blood flow is mechanically supported. Following the hypothermic phase, the patient undergoes a carefully controlled rewarming process, gradually bringing the body temperature back to normal physiological levels [ ] . This phase was equally critical as it involved the restoration of the body’s metabolic activities and the stabilization of enzymatic functions, which were temperature-dependent [ ] . The precision in managing these temperature transitions is crucial, as the thermal shifts are closely tied to endothelial function, which plays a pivotal role in regulating vascular tone, blood flow, and inflammatory responses within the body [ , ] . The endothelium, a thin layer of cells lining the blood vessels, is highly sensitive to temperature changes. Its ability to adapt to the rapid cooling and subsequent rewarming can significantly impact vascular resistance, the force against which the heart must pump blood. Changes in vascular resistance during CPB can lead to variations in blood flow and pressure that are critical to patient stability and the success of the surgical procedure [ ] . Moreover, the endothelium’s response to temperature modulations affects the release of various biochemical mediators that control inflammation, coagulation, and overall vascular health [ , ] . Therefore, understanding how these temperature phases influence endothelial function and vascular resistance is fundamental in optimizing CPB protocols and improving surgical outcomes [ ] . This introductory discussion sets the stage for a deeper exploration of the mechanisms by which temperature manipulation during CPB affects endothelial dynamics, the implications of individual variability in these responses, and how tailored clinical interventions can potentially mitigate risks and enhance recovery in cardiac surgery patients [ ] . Through a comprehensive review of current practices and ongoing research, this article aims to highlight the critical importance of thermal management in CPB and its far-reaching impacts on patient care and recovery. Endothelial function and temperature modulation Mechanisms of endothelial reactivity during cooling During CPB, the controlled reduction of body temperature to a range between 28°C and 32°C is a critical intervention designed to significantly lower the body’s metabolic rate. This therapeutic cooling was strategically implemented to protect vital organs and tissues from ischemic damage during the period when the heart’s normal pumping function is halted and replaced by the mechanical support of the bypass machine [ ] . At these lower temperatures, the biochemical and physiological processes within the body slow down considerably, which helped in reducing the consumption of oxygen and the production of metabolic waste, thereby minimizing the risk of tissue damage due to reduced blood flow. One of the key effects of this cooling is on the endothelial cells that line the blood vessels. Endothelial cells are responsible for the regulation of vascular tone through the synthesis and release of various vasoactive substances, including nitric oxide (NO), a potent vasodilator. NO is synthesized by endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), an enzyme whose activity is highly temperature-sensitive [ , ] . Cooling leads to a decrease in eNOS activity, which in turn causes a reduction in NO production. Since NO plays a crucial role in causing vasodilation, its reduced availability directly leads to an increase in vascular resistance. This increase can compromise blood flow to various organs, potentially leading to adverse outcomes if not properly managed [ ] . Moreover, the physiological response to cooling is not uniform across all individuals undergoing CPB. There is considerable variability in how different people’s endothelial cells react to reduced temperatures, which can be attributed to several factors. Genetic variations can influence the expression levels and functional efficiency of eNOS, thereby affecting the baseline and stress-induced production of NO [ ] . Additionally, individuals with pre-existing vascular conditions such as atherosclerosis or hypertension may have endothelial cells that are already compromised in their ability to produce NO, making them more susceptible to further reductions during cooling. Additionally, individuals with pre-existing vascular conditions such as atherosclerosis or hypertension may have endothelial cells that are already compromised in their ability to produce NO, making them more susceptible to further reductions during cooling. Adaptive cellular mechanisms also play a role in modulating the endothelial response to cooling. In some cases, other vasodilatory pathways might be upregulated to compensate for the decrease in NO production. For example, the production of prostacyclin, another vasodilator synthesized by endothelial cells, may increase as a compensatory response [ ] . Alternatively, changes in the handling of intracellular calcium, which is crucial for the activation of eNOS, could also help maintain some level of NO production despite the cold-induced inhibition. Understanding these mechanisms and how they vary among different patients is essential for optimizing the management of CPB, as it allows for more precise control of vascular resistance and better protection of organ function during surgery. Tailoring cooling strategies to the individual’s specific endothelial response profile may help mitigate the risks associated with reduced NO production and ensure more stable and effective outcomes from the CPB procedure. Endothelial challenges during rewarming Rewarming during CPB is a critical phase that involves carefully raising the body’s core temperature back to normal physiological levels after a period of therapeutic hypothermia [ ] . This stage was intended to reactivate the body’s metabolic functions that have been deliberately slowed during the cooling phase. While necessary, the rewarming process must be meticulously controlled to prevent thermal shock and the associated risks. One of the primary challenges during this phase is the management of oxidative stress caused by the sudden influx of oxygen to tissues that were previously under hypoxic conditions [ ] . As the body temperature rises, cellular metabolic activities accelerate, which lead to an increased demand for oxygen. This increased oxygen consumption can lead to the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are chemically reactive molecules containing oxygen. Under normal circumstances, the body’s antioxidant defenses can neutralize ROS, preventing damage. However, during the rapid rewarming in CPB, the sudden surge in ROS production can overwhelm these defenses, resulting in significant oxidative stress [ ] . This stress can damage cellular components, including lipids, proteins, and DNA, which can severely impair cellular functions. The endothelium, the inner lining of blood vessels, is particularly susceptible to oxidative damage. The endothelial cells play a crucial role in maintaining vascular health by regulating blood vessel tone, blood flow, and the balance of coagulation and fibrinolysis [ ] . Oxidative stress can impair these functions by damaging the endothelial cells, leading to dysfunction. This dysfunction can manifest as an inability to produce sufficient amounts of vasodilators such as NO, which is essential for maintaining vascular tone and ensuring proper blood flow. The resulting decrease in NO availability can cause an increase in vascular resistance, making it more difficult for the heart to pump blood efficiently through the vessels. Furthermore, the endothelium’s impaired response can lead to an increased tendency for vasoconstriction and thrombosis, contributing to elevated vascular resistance and potentially compromising the perfusion of vital organs [ ] . This situation can be particularly detrimental in the postoperative period, as it may lead to suboptimal tissue perfusion and oxygenation, increasing the risk of organ dysfunction and prolonging recovery times. To counteract these challenges, it is crucial for the rewarming process to be gradual and well-controlled to allow endothelial cells time to adapt and restore their function progressively. Monitoring endothelial biomarkers during rewarming could provide valuable insights into endothelial health and help guide the adjustment of rewarming rates and other therapeutic interventions. Pharmacological strategies may also be employed to support endothelial function during this vulnerable time. Antioxidants, for example, can be administered to help neutralize ROS and reduce oxidative stress, while vasodilators can help maintain blood flow despite potential endothelial dysfunction. Each of these elements plays a crucial role in how the endothelium reacts to the stresses imposed by CPB, particularly the extremes of cooling and rewarming, and understanding these influences is key to optimizing patient outcomes during and after surgery [ ] . At the genetic level, variations in the DNA sequences of genes encoding for endothelial nitric eNOS and other critical enzymes involved in vascular regulation can significantly impact their expression and function. At the genetic level, variations in the DNA sequences of genes encoding for endothelial nitric eNOS and other critical enzymes involved in vascular regulation can significantly impact their expression and function. Single nucleotide polymorphisms within the eNOS gene, for example, can alter enzyme activity and thus the production of NO, a pivotal mediator of vascular tone and reactivity. Reduced or enhanced functionality of this enzyme directly influences how the endothelium can cope with the induced hypothermia and subsequent rewarming of CPB, affecting vascular resistance and overall vascular health [ ] . Beyond eNOS, genetic variations in other pathways related to oxidative stress response, inflammation, and cellular repair mechanisms also contribute to the individual’s unique endothelial response profile. Physiological factors such as the presence of pre-existing medical conditions play a significant role in determining baseline endothelial health. Diseases like diabetes and hypertension are known to impair endothelial function through mechanisms involving chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and the disruption of normal NO signaling [ ] . These conditions predispose the endothelium to further dysfunction during the stress of CPB, making it more challenging to manage vascular tone and protect against ischemic injury effectively. Additionally, the overall vascular health can also be affected by lifestyle factors such as diet, smoking, and exercise, which may alter endothelial responsiveness indirectly through changes in systemic inflammation and oxidative stress levels. Age is another critical factor influencing endothelial function [ , ] . As individuals age, there is a natural decline in endothelial health, marked by a decrease in cellular reparative capacity and an increase in the propensity for arterial stiffness. These changes are compounded by the cumulative effects of longer exposure to risk factors such as elevated cholesterol levels, high blood pressure, and hyperglycemia. The aged endothelium is typically less resilient to temperature-induced stress, often exhibiting a reduced capacity to upregulate protective responses during CPB, which may necessitate more cautious management of temperature transitions and more aggressive protective strategies. Emerging evidence suggests that there are gender-specific differences in endothelial function, which may be attributed to hormonal influences. Estrogen, for instance, is known to exert protective effects on the endothelium, enhancing NO production and reducing oxidative stress [17]. This hormonal effect might explain why pre-menopausal women tend to have better endothelial function compared to men of the same age. Understanding these differences is crucial for tailoring CPB protocols, as men and women may require different management strategies to optimize endothelial protection and ensure the best surgical outcomes. Clinical management implications Personalized CPB Protocols Incorporating Minimally Invasive Extracorporeal Circulation (MiECC) The intricate nature of endothelial responses during CPB underscores the need for highly personalized CPB protocols, especially when implementing minimally invasive extracorporeal circulation (MiECC) systems. MiECC represents a significant advancement in CPB technology, focusing on reducing the invasiveness of traditional extracorporeal circulation methods, thereby minimizing the associated physiological stress and improving patient outcomes. This approach is particularly beneficial in managing the delicate balance of endothelial function during the perioperative period. Personalized protocols began with detailed preoperative assessments of endothelial function [ ] . These assessments included biomarkers of endothelial health such as levels of circulating endothelial cells, nitric oxide, and markers of inflammation and coagulation. Advanced imaging techniques may also be used to assess vascular reactivity and integrity [ , ] . By establishing a baseline of endothelial function, clinicians can better anticipate how a patient might respond to the stresses of CPB and plan accordingly. Temperature management is a critical aspect of CPB that directly impacts endothelial function. Personalized protocols, particularly when using MiECC systems, allow for more precise control over the patient’s core temperature, reducing the risk of thermal shock to the endothelium. The MiECC’s enhanced control capabilities facilitate gradual and controlled cooling and rewarming phases, which are adjusted based on the individual’s specific endothelial response patterns observed during the preoperative assessment [ ] . This method helps maintain optimal endothelial function and vascular tone throughout the procedure. In addition to tailored temperature management, personalized CPB protocols can include customized pharmacological support aimed at bolstering endothelial health. Depending on the individual’s baseline endothelial function and response to CPB, the pharmacological regimen might include antioxidants to combat oxidative stress, anti-inflammatory agents to reduce endothelial inflammation, or vasodilators to support NO production and maintain vascular tone [ , ] . The use of these agents can be finely tuned in real-time, guided by continuous monitoring of endothelial markers and vascular resistance. Pharmacological enhancements in cardiopulmonary bypass In the realm of CPB, the strategic use of pharmacological agents is crucial for managing and mitigating the impact of temperature fluctuations on endothelial function. As CPB can significantly stress the endothelium through induced hypothermia and subsequent rewarming, targeted pharmacological interventions are essential to maintain endothelial integrity and function [ ] . This section elaborated on the rationale, types, and personalized application of these pharmacological enhancements, focusing on NO donors, endothelial protective agents, and antioxidants. During CPB, especially in the phases of cooling and rewarming, endothelial cells are exposed to conditions that can lead to dysfunction, primarily due to reduced production of endothelium-derived vasodilators such as NO, increased oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses. Pharmacological agents that can directly or indirectly modulate these factors were thus considered vital in maintaining vascular health and ensuring adequate tissue perfusion during and after surgery [ ] . Types of pharmacological agents (1) Nitric oxide donors: Nitric oxide donors are compounds that release NO within the body. NO is a fundamental mediator of vascular tone and is essential for preventing platelet aggregation and leukocyte adhesion to the endothelium, which are common during CPB. By supplementing NO through pharmacological means, it is possible to counteract the reduced endogenous NO production caused by cooling. Agents such as nitroglycerin and sodium nitroprusside are commonly used for their vasodilatory effects, which can help maintain blood flow and reduce vascular resistance [ , ] . (2) L-arginine supplementation: L-arginine is a semi-essential amino acid and a direct substrate for eNOS in the synthesis of nitric oxide. Supplementing with L-arginine during CPB can support endogenous NO production, particularly in patients with endothelial dysfunction or limited eNOS activity. Its benefits have been observed in both adult and pediatric populations undergoing hypothermic CPB, where it helps restore vascular tone and improve tissue perfusion [ , ] . (3) Endothelial protective agents: This category includes drugs that specifically target and mitigate endothelial cell injury. Agents such as statins and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors have shown promise in protecting the endothelium by reducing inflammatory responses and oxidative stress, and by enhancing the bioavailability of NO. Statins, for example, have been observed to improve endothelial function by their cholesterol-lowering effects and their ability to modulate eNOS activity [ , ] . (4) Antioxidants: Antioxidants play a critical role in neutralizing ROS generated during the rewarming phase of CPB. Excessive ROS can lead to oxidative stress, damaging endothelial cells and leading to further vascular dysfunction. Antioxidants such as vitamin C, vitamin E, and N-acetylcysteine can help mitigate this damage by scavenging free radicals and supporting the natural antioxidant defense systems of the body [ ] . This personalized approach begins with a detailed preoperative evaluation of the patient’s vascular health, including assessments of endothelial function and markers of inflammation and oxidative stress [ ] . Continuing pharmacological management after CPB is crucial for supporting endothelial recovery and reducing the risk of complications such as postoperative vasospasm or inflammation. Optimizing temperature transitions in cardiopulmonary bypass The management of temperature transitions during CPB is a critical component of the procedure that requires meticulous planning and execution. Gradual and controlled adjustments in temperature are essential to minimize endothelial stress and prevent abrupt changes in vascular resistance, which can adversely affect patient outcomes. This section explores the importance of optimizing temperature transitions, the technologies involved, and the methodologies for implementing effective temperature control during CPB [ ] . Temperature transitions during CPB, including both cooling and rewarming phases, must be managed with precision to protect the endothelium and maintain hemodynamic stability. Rapid changes in temperature can lead to thermal shock, which can cause cellular stress and trigger inflammatory responses that compromise endothelial function and increase vascular resistance [ , ] . Such changes not only affect the immediate surgical outcomes but also have long-term implications for patient recovery and health. The advancement of thermal management systems in CPB has been significant [ ] . These systems are designed to offer precise control over the patient’s body temperature, allowing for gradual temperature changes that align with the body’s natural physiological responses: (1) Temperature control devices: Modern temperature control devices used in CPB include heat exchangers and warming/cooling blankets that can be adjusted in real-time to regulate the patient’s core temperature. These devices are often integrated with feedback systems that monitor the patient’s temperature continuously and adjust heating or cooling outputs automatically [ ] . (2) Algorithmic temperature modulation: Some advanced systems employ algorithms that predict how a patient’s temperature should be adjusted based on a variety of factors, including the initial body temperature, the duration of the surgery, and specific patient characteristics. These algorithms help in achieving more personalized temperature control, tailored to each patient’s unique physiological profile [ ] . (3) Sensor-based feedback systems: Integrating sensor-based technology to provide real-time data on the patient’s physiological state is another leap forward. These sensors can detect slight changes in body temperature, fluid balance, and hemodynamic parameters, allowing for immediate adjustments to the temperature control strategy [ , ] . Methodologies for effective temperature management To effectively manage temperature transitions during CPB, a structured methodology should be employed that encompasses preoperative planning, intraoperative management, and postoperative care: (1) Preoperative planning: Before initiating CPB, a comprehensive plan should be developed based on the patient’s medical history, underlying conditions, and specific surgical requirements. This plan should outline the target temperature range for each phase of the surgery and define the rate at which temperature changes will be effected [ , ] . (2) Intraoperative temperature management: During the surgery, continuous monitoring is crucial. The temperature should be adjusted gradually to avoid rapid shifts that could lead to vascular instability [ ] . (3) Postoperative monitoring and adjustment: After the surgery, careful monitoring must continue during the recovery phase. The rewarming process should be completed slowly to ensure that the body adjusts without undue stress. Postoperative temperature management also includes monitoring for and addressing any delayed effects of temperature fluctuations, such as shivering or hyperthermia, which can affect recovery [ ] . Conclusions The management of temperature transitions during CPB is critical for ensuring the best possible outcomes in cardiac surgery. This editorial highlighted the intricate relationship between endothelial reactivity to temperature changes and vascular resistance, demonstrating how precise control over these elements is essential for maintaining endothelial function and optimizing patient recovery. Personalized CPB protocols, which take into account individual variations in endothelial response due to genetic, physiological, and demographic factors, are crucial for tailoring treatment to meet specific patient needs. Background Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) represents a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance, impaired insulin secretion, and persistent hyperglycemia ( ). The global burden of this condition is substantial, with the World Health Organization reporting that T2DM accounts for more than 90% of all diabetes cases worldwide ( ). Current epidemiological data indicate that approximately 537 million adults were affected in 2021, with projections suggesting this figure will escalate to 783 million by 2045 ( ). Notably, the prevalence in China has reached 12.4% among adults as of 2018, surpassing the global average ( ). The clinical significance of T2DM extends beyond glycemic disturbances, as it frequently precipitates devastating complications including cardiovascular disease, nephropathy, retinopathy, and neuropathy, collectively contributing to substantial morbidity and diminished quality of life ( ). Constipation constitutes a prevalent gastrointestinal disorder defined by infrequent bowel movements or difficulty with defecation, typically diagnosed according to Rome IV criteria ( ). The prevalence of constipation among T2DM patients demonstrates a striking disparity, ranging from 30 to 60%, which markedly exceeds the approximately 14% prevalence observed in the general population ( , ). This elevated risk primarily stems from diabetic autonomic neuropathy. In addition, multiple contributing factors further compound this association, including delayed gastric emptying, sedentary lifestyle patterns, inadequate fiber, and fluid consumption, adverse medication effects, and disrupted gut microbiota homeostasis ( ). Furthermore, constipation may compromise glycemic management through impaired drug absorption and reduced dietary adherence. Despite its clinical relevance, constipation remains significantly underaddressed in diabetes care protocols, with numerous patients either dismissing symptoms or resorting to prolonged, unsupervised laxative use, potentially exacerbating clinical outcomes ( ). These observations highlight the critical need for systematic educational initiatives and behavior-oriented interventions to enhance constipation management within comprehensive T2DM care. The Knowledge, Attitude, and Practice (KAP) framework serves as a validated diagnostic research instrument that elucidates individuals' comprehension, perceptions, and behavioral patterns concerning specific health conditions ( , ). Within health literacy research, the KAP model operates on the theoretical premise that knowledge acquisition influences attitudinal formation, which subsequently determines behavioral practices ( ). This methodological approach has demonstrated extensive utility in chronic disease investigations, particularly diabetes research, where it has been employed to evaluate patient engagement in critical self-management activities including blood glucose monitoring, dietary adherence, and preventive foot care ( , ). The majority of existing KAP investigations have concentrated on well-established diabetic complications such as diabetic foot ulceration or general diabetes self-management, consistently revealing that patients frequently exhibit suboptimal practices despite possessing adequate theoretical knowledge ( , ). However, the application of this framework to gastrointestinal complications—particularly constipation, which represents a highly prevalent yet consistently underrecognized complication in T2DM—remains notably limited. To bridge this knowledge gap, the present cross-sectional investigation systematically examines the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of patients with T2DM regarding constipation management. By employing a validated behavioral assessment framework, this study seeks to generate robust, generalizable, and patient-centered evidence that will inform the development of targeted educational interventions and enhance constipation management protocols within comprehensive diabetes care. Methods Study design and participants This cross-sectional study was conducted between October 2024 and May 2025 at Gansu Provincial Hospital. Patients with T2DM were invited to complete questionnaires. The inclusion criteria were: (1) meeting the diagnostic criteria for type 2 diabetes mellitus according to the American Diabetes Association (ADA) guidelines. Exclusion criteria were: (1) patients with severe primary diseases, including advanced or decompensated cardiac dysfunction, severe hepatic impairment, or advanced renal dysfunction requiring intensive medical management, as well as hematopoietic system disorders or psychiatric disorders; (2) individuals lacking legal capacity or insight, or those unable to understand or complete the questionnaire. This study received an ethics exemption from the Ethics Committee of Gansu Provincial Hospital and obtained informed consent from all participants prior to the start of the research. Glycemic control status was classified according to ADA recommendations. Patients with glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels < 7.0% were defined as having controlled diabetes, whereas those with HbA1c levels ≥7.0% were classified as uncontrolled. Glycemic control treatment was provided according to routine clinical practice and current guideline recommendations, including lifestyle modification and pharmacological therapy such as oral hypoglycemic agents and/or insulin. Information on antidiabetic treatment was collected from medical records; however, treatment regimens were not used as stratification variables in the main statistical analyses.
